epigraph.quote: We have built a strong platform; our task now is to deliver on its potential.
epigraph.author: Afzal Malkani, Managing Director [1]

web_blocks.text: TANFAC’s history is best read as a series of operating transitions within one chemistry family, rather than as a sequence of unrelated diversifications. The company reports commercial production beginning in March 1985 at its Cuddalore complex, initially with hydrofluoric acid (HF), aluminium fluoride and sulphuric acid. The subsequent record includes HF liquefaction and specialty fluoride production in the late 1980s, a sulphuric-acid expansion and captive power in 2002, and further inorganic-fluoride and specialty-chemistry work through 2004–20. The FY26 annual report gives an incorporation year of 1972, while ICRA’s company history gives 1974; the sources therefore do not agree on the incorporation date, but both place the manufacturing platform’s start in the 1980s. [1][2][7]

An independent retrospective profile attributes a severe downturn and minimal operations to the global subprime crisis and strong Chinese competition.
This is a retrospective profile, not an audited operating series; the allowed evidence does not quantify the downturn. [9]
March 2022 onward
Anupam Rasayan joined TIDCO as co-promoter; management describes a move from stabilization to capacity expansion, downstream products and stronger technical/customer access.
Ownership change is a management-reported inflection, not proof that every later project has already earned its intended return. [1][3][7]
October 2024–FY26
Expanded HF capacity was commissioned; both solar-grade DHF phases were commissioned in June and October 2025; an HFC-32 project entered implementation.
HF and solar-grade DHF are operating assets; HFC-32 remained a project under construction at the latest supplied call. [1][2][3][6]

web_blocks.text: The post-2022 sequence is concrete. The expanded HF plant was commissioned in October 2024, increasing reported capacity from about 14,850 to 30,000 tonnes per year. Two 10,000-tonne-per-year solar-grade diluted HF (DHF) phases followed in June and October 2025. FY26 was a record year for revenue and production, but the company also described FY25’s unusually strong realizations as a temporary demand–supply gap; higher sulphur costs and depreciation on new assets then coincided with lower FY26 operating margins. This is a business-cycle lesson: capacity additions can lift output and sales while input spreads and depreciation pull earnings in the opposite direction. [1][2][3]

You should keep the longer-cycle evidence in proportion. The CEO Magazine profile says that global turmoil in 2007 and strong Chinese competition left TANFAC with minimal operations; it offers historical context but does not provide audited annual figures. The current public record is richer for FY23–FY27 than for the earlier period. It supports a narrative of past disruption, a later ownership and operating reset, and a new build-out, but not a quantified decade-long cycle comparison. [9][1][2][6]

web_blocks.title: The distinction to preserve
paragraphs: A commissioned plant, an announced project, a customer order and a profitable ramp are four different milestones. The HF and solar-grade DHF plants have moved into operation; the refrigerant-gas facility was still progressing toward commissioning in the latest supplied transcript. Treat these as separate evidence states. [1][6]

web_blocks.text: A more precise chronology helps separate what the company has actually built from what it now intends to build. The audited FY26 report places the early platform at Cuddalore: commercial production began in March 1985, with hydrofluoric acid, aluminium fluoride and sulphuric acid. The investor presentation adds HF liquefaction in 1987, specialty fluoride production in 1989, sulphuric-acid expansion and a captive power plant in 2002, and diversification into inorganic fluorides and specialty organic chemicals across 2004–20. The annual report states incorporation in 1972, while ICRA’s profile says 1974; that discrepancy should remain visible rather than be silently resolved. Both accounts place the operating base in the same Cuddalore industrial complex. [1][2][7]

web_blocks.text: The recent financial arc shows why this chronology should not be mistaken for a smooth secular climb. The company reports revenue from operations of ₹374.95 crore in FY23, ₹378.15 crore in FY24, ₹556.98 crore in FY25 and ₹711.07 crore in FY26. Revenue accelerated after capacity additions, but operating EBITDA moved from ₹74.76 crore to ₹70.72 crore, then ₹128.86 crore and ₹112.06 crore. FY25’s margin benefited from a temporary demand–supply gap and unusually high realizations, especially in one quarter; in FY26, higher raw-material costs and new depreciation accompanied the new revenue record. The sequence is consistent with a capacity-led chemical business whose results also depend on spreads and mix. [1][2][3]

web_blocks.caption: A short, source-backed cycle map; the 2007 account is retrospective rather than audited. [1][2][3][7][9]
rows: Historical disruption
CEO Magazine retrospectively says the 2007 global subprime crisis and strong Chinese competition pushed TANFAC into a severe downturn and minimal operations.
Treat as a warning about demand and competition, not as a measured margin or revenue series; the source does not audit or quantify the episode. [9]
Operating reset
After Anupam Rasayan joined in 2022, the company describes stabilization, upgraded R&D, a pilot plant and improved operating execution.
Ownership and technical access can support execution, but are not substitutes for evidence of output, utilization and cash generation. [1][2][3]
Demand / spread upswing
FY25 produced record financial results, with management attributing unusually strong realizations to temporary tight supply.
A peak margin year can overstate through-cycle profitability if the supply-demand imbalance is temporary. [1][3]
Capacity plus normalization
FY26 revenue and production set records, while EBITDA margin moderated from 23.14% to 15.76% and PAT margin from 15.83% to 9.86%.
Volume growth, margin normalization and depreciation can move in different directions. [1][2]

web_blocks.text: The five-year revenue statement is also narrower than it first appears. The annual report gives a FY21 revenue point of about ₹147.90 crore and FY26 revenue of ₹711.07 crore, described by the Board as close to a fivefold increase. It does not provide a full audited FY17–FY26 income, cash-flow and balance-sheet series in the supplied material. Nor does the CEO Magazine profile fill that gap: it is a qualitative retrospective. You can responsibly say that scale expanded substantially from the disclosed FY21 point, and that the FY23–FY26 series shows acceleration; you cannot claim that every intervening year compounded smoothly or that the last four years represent a complete cycle. [1][2][9]

The ownership transition is operationally relevant but should be parsed carefully. TANFAC remains a joint-sector company with TIDCO and Anupam Rasayan as co-promoters; ICRA says Anupam has management control and is strategically linked through fluorination. Management credits the relationship with technical expertise, specialty-chemistry capability and access to global customers. The development path since 2022 has remained within fluorine chemistry: expand HF, add a high-purity grade, and prepare for a refrigerant-gas step. This is a coherent adjacency strategy. It is not yet proof that all future applications will share the same unit economics, customer qualification duration or working-capital profile. [1][3][7]

web_blocks.title: Counterfactual test: what if the cycle turns before the new platform matures?
paragraphs: If commodity HF demand or customer activity weakens, existing high core utilization may fall before newer downstream products reach repeatable scale. If raw-material costs rise faster than contractual pass-through, revenue can grow while percentage margins compress; management describes a lag, and ICRA flags spread volatility. If competition adds capacity, first-mover status alone may not defend commodity economics. A sound history therefore gives weight to both the completed HF / solar-grade projects and the older evidence of cyclicality. [1][3][6][7][9]

book_paragraphs: When you study TANFAC, begin with the molecule and the site, not with the latest growth narrative. The company’s industrial identity has been built around hydrofluoric acid, sulphuric acid and derivatives made at Cuddalore. That continuity matters because it explains why later moves into higher-purity DHF and refrigerant gas are adjacent extensions of existing process knowledge. It does not make the new products risk-free: a downstream product brings customer qualification, operating stability and commercial ramp requirements of its own. [1][2]

You should also distinguish an operating history from a complete historical dataset. The independent retrospective account describes a genuine severe downturn associated with the 2007 global crisis and Chinese competition, but it is not an audited series. The better evidenced recent chapter begins with Anupam Rasayan’s 2022 entry as co-promoter, followed by the HF expansion and solar-grade DHF commissioning. Management’s words—“our task now is to deliver on its potential”—are a useful test to carry forward: the platform is established, while delivery of the newest projects still has to be demonstrated in operating results. [9][1][3][6]

You should read the company’s life in layers. The first layer is industrial continuity: Cuddalore, hydrofluoric acid, sulphuric acid and fluorine derivatives. The second is capability accumulation: liquefaction, specialty fluorides, captive power and later R&D and pilot facilities. The third is the recent downstream turn, which depends on the old platform but adds new qualification and commercialization demands. This sequence makes strategic sense because the company is not leaving its chemistry behind; it is trying to create more value from it. But coherence of direction is only the beginning of an operating case. For each new layer, ask whether the asset exists, whether customers have qualified it, whether output is stable, and whether cash is being earned after the capital is committed. [1][2][3][6]

The historical record also teaches you not to use a peak year as the default. The CEO Magazine retrospective attributes a severe downturn and minimal operations to the combined effect of the 2007 global crisis and Chinese competition. That account is not an audited dataset, so do not turn it into a fabricated revenue curve. It is still a useful stress case: fluorochemical demand can contract or shift, and competitors can alter market economics. In more recent years, FY25’s unusually favorable realizations lifted margins; FY26 brought higher raw-material costs and depreciation on newer assets. The business can expand physically while its margin profile normalizes. [9][1][3]

When you examine the Anupam Rasayan era, separate the enabling conditions from the outcome. A co-promoter with fluorine expertise and customer reach may help TANFAC develop products and execute projects. The HF expansion and solar-grade DHF commissioning provide concrete evidence of delivery. The annual report’s revenue point for FY21 and four-year FY23–FY26 figures show substantial recent scale growth, but the record supplied here does not contain a decade of audited financial statements. An institutionally careful account says exactly that: the recent platform has grown, while the complete pre- and post-cycle financial picture is unavailable in the allowed evidence. [1][2][7]

Your best historical question is therefore not “How fast did it grow?” but “Under what conditions did the growth occur, and what had to be true for it to continue?” FY25 shows how a temporary supply-demand gap can raise realizations; FY26 shows how input costs and depreciation can dilute the conversion of extra revenue into profit. If a new product is not yet commissioned or qualified, it cannot automatically offset a downturn in a core line. Use the past as a set of conditions and counterfactuals, not as an extrapolation template. Management’s phrase—“our task now is to deliver on its potential”—is a fair summary of the gap between a credible platform and a completed growth cycle. [1][3][6]

One way to test the historical story is to compare the quality of each milestone, not just the date. An installed HF unit gives capacity; a high utilization figure shows it is being used; record production says the operating system handled that volume; cash generation tells you whether the activity funded itself. For the solar-grade DHF line, commissioning is followed by customer trials, order coverage and later debottlenecking. For HFC-32, the evidence in the supplied period reaches construction progress and supply arrangements, but not operating output. These are different rungs. If you compress them into “the company has transformed,” you lose the practical distinction between the proven base and the next proof point. [1][2][4][6]

You can also test whether the new phase genuinely diversifies the old one. The strategy retains common fluorine chemistry and draws on captive HF, which offers technical adjacency. But solar wafer customers, HVAC buyers and specialty chemical customers do not have identical approval processes or demand cycles. A solar-grade line can depend on cell manufacturing capacity; a refrigerant line depends on cooling demand and the applicable HFC phase-down framework; commodity acids remain exposed to industrial cycles. The portfolio may broaden end markets while still concentrating operationally in one chemistry, one site and a set of related feedstocks. That is a more precise claim than saying the business is simply diversified. [1][2][7][10]

A final historical discipline is to keep corporate chronology separate from operating continuity. The incorporation-year discrepancy in the permitted company and ICRA accounts does not change the better-supported fact that commercial manufacturing at Cuddalore began in 1985. Likewise, a later ownership change is an event, while improved operation is a claim that should be tested against production, utilization and cash. The available evidence supports both the company’s description of a reset after 2022 and the independent profile’s account of prior disruption, but it does not supply a complete annual bridge between them. You can tell that history honestly without smoothing the uncertain years into a seamless narrative. [1][2][7][9]

The transition also needs a disciplined definition of “cycle.” Here it means changes in industrial demand, input spreads, utilization and operating profitability—not movements in the company’s shares. The permitted evidence includes an attributed historical downturn, a recent exceptional realization period and later margin normalization. It does not include enough annual data to measure a complete cycle statistically. You can still compare the contrasting operating regimes, but keep the 2007 account qualitative, use the audited FY23–FY26 financial series for numerical comparison, and label management explanations as management explanations. [1][2][3][9]

book_callouts.title: Reflection — continuity versus proof
book_callouts.text: Which parts of the growth story are extensions of operating capabilities already proven at Cuddalore, and which still depend on qualification, commissioning or customer ramp? Keep those two lists separate when you assess evidence. [1][6]
